cards.title: End User Authoring of Personalized Content Classifiers: Comparing Example Labeling, Rule Writing, and LLM Prompting

quotes: "To make creating personal classifiers for content curation easier for such users, tools should support rapid initialization and iterative refinement." (p. 1)

"Through pilot studies (detailed in Appendix A), we iteratively implemented three systems corresponding to the three primary teaching vocabularies: Label System (labeling examples to train a supervised model), Rule System (writing executable rules), and Prompt System (writing prompts for an LLM)." (p. 5)
"Then, in each condition, participants were given 15 minutes to create classifiers." (p. 9)
"Fourth, our study was conducted solely in English and focused on political content, limiting its applicability to other languages and types of content." (p. 17)

claim_entries.value: prompt authoring produced superior classifier performance more rapidly, driven by recall, while later refinement remained difficult (PDF p. 11).
quotes: "In summary, the Prompt System enabled end users to create custom moderation classifiers with superior performance more rapidly compared to the other two systems." (p. 11)

"Temporally, we observed that the Prompt System facilitated rapid classifier initialization during the early stage but faced challenges in supporting further iteration, as evidenced by its plateaued precision and recall afterward." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: within_subject — three randomized authoring-system conditions (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "We employed a within-subjects design with the three experiment systems described above." (p. 8)
"We recruited 37 participants with no programming experience by advertising a call for participation on mailing lists of non-Computer Science departments at two major U.S.-based universities." (p. 8)

claim_entries.value: general_students — most participants were university students outside computer science (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "Most participants were pursuing their bachelor’s degrees except four pursuing more advanced degrees." (p. 8)

claim_entries.value: baseline_system — the other two authoring systems served as within-subject comparators (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "We employed a within-subjects design with the three experiment systems described above." (p. 8)

claim_entries.value: effect_size_and_test — pairwise estimated differences and significance tests were reported (PDF p. 11).
quotes: "However, Prompt System showed significantly higher recall compared to both Label System (Est.Diff = 0.205, 𝑝 < 0.001) and the Rule System (Est.Diff = 0.232, 𝑝 < 0.001)." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: three 25-minute conditions in one approximately 100-129-minute session, with 15 minutes of classifier creation per condition (PDF pp. 8-9).
quotes: "The individual user studies averaged 129 minutes in length, while the in-person workshops lasted about 100 minutes." (p. 8)
"Each condition lasted 25 minutes in total." (p. 9)
"Then, in each condition, participants were given 15 minutes to create classifiers." (p. 9)

claim_entries.value: accuracy did not differ significantly; rule and prompt precision plateaued or decreased; overall system preference did not differ significantly (PDF pp. 11, 14).
quotes: "We do not observe significant differences in accuracy between the systems." (p. 11)
"While both the Prompt System and the Rule System showed notable improvements in recall by the end of the experiment, their precision either plateaued or even decreased over time." (p. 11)
"The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test showed no significant differences between any of the systems." (p. 14)

claim_entries.value: the within-subject estimates support the bounded performance claim, while the authors appropriately limit transfer beyond a small undergraduate, English-language political-content study (PDF p. 17).
quotes: "Besides, our participant pool of undergraduates did not represent the diverse population of internet users, and our study involved a relatively small number of participants." (p. 17)
"Fourth, our study was conducted solely in English and focused on political content, limiting its applicability to other languages and types of content." (p. 17)

paper_code_entries.value: personalized social-media content moderation and end-user classifier authoring — (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "They were then invited to set up automated classifiers to remove unwanted content based on their personal preferences." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: immediate_performance_or_sensemaking — the support targets rapid creation and iterative improvement of a working classifier (PDF p. 1).
quotes: "To make creating personal classifiers for content curation easier for such users, tools should support rapid initialization and iterative refinement." (p. 1)

paper_code_entries.value: novice_or_learner — participants had no programming experience and little algorithm knowledge (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "We recruited 37 participants with no programming experience by advertising a call for participation on mailing lists of non-Computer Science departments at two major U.S.-based universities." (p. 8)
"We only selected participants who self-reported having little knowledge of programming and algorithms." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: strategy_or_process_gap — users had preferences but struggled with how to teach the classifier or diagnose failure (PDF p. 4).
quotes: "For instance, users might struggle to find effective ways to teach the algorithm (i.e., use barrier) or diagnose why the algorithm fails (i.e., understanding barriers) [48]." (p. 4)

paper_code_entries.value: process — interactions and subjective authoring experience were measured (PDF p. 9).
quotes: "We documented 23 different types of user interactions, including asking for synonym suggestions, loading additional examples, and applying classifiers to examples." (p. 9)

paper_code_entries.value: artifact — classifier quality was measured (PDF p. 9).
quotes: "To determine which system could learn user preferences with the highest performance, we evaluated the accuracy, precision, recall, and 𝐹1 score of the final systems participants developed." (p. 9)

paper_code_entries.value: structuring — rules organize preferences into explicit conjunctive and exception conditions (PDF p. 7).
quotes: "which are combined with a logical AND" (p. 7)
"to specify an exception, such as keeping texts about gun rights" (p. 7)

paper_code_entries.value: problematizing — prediction review makes problematic prompts and mistakes available for reflection rather than hiding them (PDF p. 14).
quotes: "Participants found that they could at least review and reflect on problematic prompts in the Prompt System, whereas they could not pinpoint specific labels that led to classification mistakes in the Label System." (p. 14)

paper_code_entries.value: contingency — the next examples depend on uncertainty after the user's current labels (PDF p. 5).
quotes: "After a user labels a set of examples, we train the algorithm on these labels and calculate the predicted positive probabilities for the remaining examples in the training dataset." (p. 5)
"We subsequently sample examples with the highest label uncertainty." (p. 5)

paper_code_entries.value: adaptation — the learned classifier updates from the person's labels (PDF p. 5).
quotes: "After a user labels a set of examples, we train the algorithm on these labels and calculate the predicted positive probabilities for the remaining examples in the training dataset." (p. 5)

paper_code_entries.value: hybrid_or_multi_model — mechanisms span supervised learning, executable rules, and LLM prompting (PDF p. 5).
quotes: "Through pilot studies (detailed in Appendix A), we iteratively implemented three systems corresponding to the three primary teaching vocabularies: Label System (labeling examples to train a supervised model), Rule System (writing executable rules), and Prompt System (writing prompts for an LLM)." (p. 5)

paper_code_entries.value: llm_era — the study's generative path uses a named GPT-4 model (PDF p. 6).
quotes: "Throughout our implementation, we used OpenAI’s gpt-4-1106-preview model." (p. 6)

limitations: "As a result, we did not have the chance to test other less common combinations in our experiments, such as supervised learning algorithms for rules (i.e., a Snorkel-like system [66])." (PDF p. 17)

"To prevent the experiments from being excessively long, we limited participants to labeling only 100 comments that comprised our test dataset, which might affect our evaluation’s accuracy." (PDF p. 17)
"Besides, our participant pool of undergraduates did not represent the diverse population of internet users, and our study involved a relatively small number of participants." (PDF p. 17)
"Fourth, our study was conducted solely in English and focused on political content, limiting its applicability to other languages and types of content." (PDF p. 17)
"Finally, while personal content moderation as a case study illustrates the primary user needs for content curation tools, we acknowledge the diversity of content curation scenarios." (PDF p. 17)
boundary_conditions: "We conducted a within-subjects experiment with 37 participants with no programming experience to comparatively evaluate these three personal moderation systems for everyday users." (PDF p. 4)
"While we focus on content-based curation in this work, end users also frequently curate content based on metadata." (PDF p. 16)
"Additionally, while our findings on binary classifiers could be generalized to a categorical classifier, they cannot be easily extended to regression algorithms." (PDF p. 16)
"Future work should examine whether there are distinct user needs in other scenarios before applying our findings broadly." (PDF p. 17)
